svg.text: The renewal pipeline: one daily tick, from alarm clock to commission engine
Every step is deterministic. The right column names the real-world failure each step makes impossible.
1. The daily tick opens a run
Fired by the scheduler at the staff-set time, or by RUN NOW in the console, with an
optional limit ("run exactly 5"). The alarm is a convenience; the run is the record.
2. Reconcile first
Before any new charge, sweep every attempt still without an answer. Ask the payment
platform for the truth; anything unresolved goes to the staff attention queue.
3. Gather everything due on or before today
Billing dates are computed fresh from the member's original anchor date, never by
adding a month to a stored date. A missed day is simply picked up by the next tick.
4. Business rules, applied at billing time
Price is read fresh from the one catalog (a subscription never stores a price).
The stored card credential passes a pre-flight coherence check before anything is sent.
A promotions hook runs (deliberately a no-op today). Each cycle is locked under a
one-billing-per-cycle database key before dispatch.
5. Dispatch the charge, cardholder absent
An order-shaped row is written, then charged as a merchant-initiated transaction.
A renewal NEVER asks an absent cardholder to answer a bank identity challenge.
6. Payment orchestrator
HyperSwitch, the same rail the
shop checkout already uses.
7. Braintree
The card processor answers:
paid, or a numbered decline code.
8. The verdict is classified from a data table, never guessed
Every decline code is labeled member-fault (the card or the cardholder) or system-fault
(our defect). Only member-fault declines may ever consume the member's retry ladder or
count toward cancellation. System faults route to the staff attention queue instead.
9. State machine and retry ladder
Paid means active. A soft decline schedules retries at +2, +4, +8, +15, +22 days, clipped
inside the calendar month. A hard decline is never retried. See the state machine diagram.
paid charges only
10. The bridge books the volume
Only processor-confirmed paid charges become volume. A quarterly charge of $300.00
spreads 100 Personal Volume (PV) into each of its three covered months.
11. Commission engine, not one line changed
It reads ordinary orders. It never learns that renewals exist.
The failure each step makes impossible
Step 2 kills the ORPHANED ORDER
An order created but never charged cannot sit
forgotten: every tick opens by hunting for exactly
that, and nothing resolves silently.
Step 3 kills the DOUBLE RELEASE and
the SILENTLY SKIPPED MONTH
Due-ness derives from the accounting of past
cycles under a unique key: a cycle already billed
is refused by the database itself, and a cycle
never billed stays due until it is. A cycle audit
view makes any gap a visible red row.
Step 4 kills STALE PRICING and the
WRONG-CARD CHARGE
A price that is never stored cannot go stale.
A credential that is one immutable record, and is
checked before dispatch, cannot point at the
wrong card without being caught first.
Step 5 keeps the card networks happy
No interactive bank challenge is ever requested
on a renewal. If one comes back anyway, the
attempt fails cleanly and the member is asked
for a fresh checkout, card in hand.
Step 8 keeps our mistakes off the
member's record
A configuration defect on our side never eats a
member's retries and never pushes them toward
auto-cancel. Run reports total the two fault
families separately so neither can hide.
Step 9 makes retries logical, not blind
The decline reason decides the retry. A stolen-card
decline is never retried; an insufficient-funds
decline waits for payday. A blind schedule does
the opposite of both.
Steps 10 and 11 make volume honest
The engine cannot invent volume even if it has a
bug: only the bridge writes orders, and the bridge
admits only processor-confirmed paid charges.
A failed month means no payment, no volume,
not qualified. No exceptions.
Proven, not promised
All of the above ran against a full simulated year
(394 daily ticks, 855 renewal cycles, each
accounted exactly once) with 75 automated proofs
passing, including a deliberate crash mid-batch,
a deliberate double-run of the same day, and a
deliberately corrupted card credential.
